items.prompt: Two completed runs return the same i8 value. One leaves A=[2], the other A=[3]. Which comparison is justified?

choices.B: Different because final heap is observable
choices.C: Unknown because all memory is excluded

items.why: All initial heap objects are observable, even when the return values agree.

items.prompt: Two runs both stop at the fuel limit after emitting the same events. What may the validator claim?
items.why: A matching finite prefix cannot establish matching completed behavior.

items.prompt: Entry branches to left or right; both reach join. A value is defined only in left and used directly in join. What is missing?

choices.A: A dominating definition or edge-correct phi

items.why: There is an entry-to-join path through right that never executes the definition.

items.prompt: A header phi reads a body-defined value only on the body-to-header backedge. Must that body definition dominate entry-to-header?

choices.A: Yes, every phi operand must dominate the header
choices.B: No, availability is checked at its own predecessor terminator
choices.C: No, phis may read any runtime slot

items.why: Each incoming value must be available on its corresponding predecessor edge.

items.prompt: An unused load reads one-past an array. Is deleting it a valid generic dead-result optimization?

choices.A: Yes, its result has no users
choices.B: Only when the array has one element
choices.C: No, deleting a possible bounds trap changes behavior

items.why: A load may trap even when nobody uses its result. Dead-result elimination here is restricted to total pure instructions.

items.prompt: Two identical total arithmetic expressions occur in different branches. Neither branch dominates the other. May one result replace the other?

choices.A: Yes, equal expression keys are enough
choices.B: No, the replacement value may be unavailable
choices.C: Only if their IDs have equal length

items.why: Expression equality and value availability are separate obligations.

items.prompt: A loop phi initially has one reachable constant input. Later a backedge carrying a different value becomes executable. What happens to the constant claim?

choices.A: It stays constant because it was found first
choices.B: It must be revised using the new incoming information

items.why: A fixed-point analysis must propagate newly available control and value facts.

items.prompt: After a proven constant branch removes an edge, a join has one incoming constant. What is the useful next action?

choices.A: Revisit that phi and its users
choices.B: Preserve all old analysis facts without checking
choices.C: Stop because only the original blocks may be optimized

items.why: Control simplification can expose new constant facts; iterate until no justified edit remains.

items.prompt: p and q are different parameter names. No input contract separates them. A store through q sits between two loads through p. What alias answer is safe?
items.why: Names do not identify runtime objects. The intervening store prevents unconditional reuse.

items.prompt: q is derived as p plus one typed element. There are no casts or byte reinterpretations. Do accesses through p and q address the same cell?

choices.B: No, the known element offsets differ
choices.C: Always unknown even with exact offsets

items.why: Object identity alone does not imply the same typed cell. Bounds safety remains a separate issue.

items.prompt: A loop-invariant pointer may reference an empty object, and the loop can execute zero times. May its load be hoisted?

choices.B: No, hoisting may introduce a bounds trap
choices.C: Yes, if the load has one use

items.why: Address invariance does not establish that executing a load earlier is safe.

items.prompt: A load address is fixed and in bounds, but the loop may store through an alias. What is still missing for load motion?

choices.A: Proof that the loaded value is not changed in the loop

items.why: A stable address can refer to changing contents.

items.prompt: A required domain has 12 inputs. Eleven pairs complete equally; the last reaches a resource limit. Which result is correct?
items.why: Required work did not finish. Do not silently remove the unfinished input.

items.prompt: A candidate lowers total modeled work on the frozen workload but raises it for zero-trip calls. What should its report do?

choices.B: Show per-input increases and aggregate decrease under the declared model

items.why: An aggregate benefit is not a worst-case improvement or measured machine speedup.

items.prompt: A reduced file now crashes the parser, while the original bug was a normal-return wrong result. Has the reducer preserved the target failure?

choices.B: No, it changed the failure predicate

items.why: Reduction must retain the specified legal miscompilation, not merely a failure.

items.prompt: One final one-step reduction times out; every other tested neighbor loses the discrepancy. May the result be called 1-minimal?

choices.B: Only if the timed-out input is small

items.why: 1-minimality requires resolving every permitted one-step neighbor of the final candidate.

items.prompt: A repair disables every optimization and returns the original program. It fixes the witness. Does it meet the capstone?

choices.A: Yes, correctness is the only criterion
choices.B: No, the repair must retain legitimate optimization wins
choices.C: Only if its source file is shorter

items.why: The project requires a useful optimizer as well as elimination of the demonstrated bug.

items.prompt: Your repaired optimizer passes a declared 48-input boundary set. Which claim is supported?

choices.C: Those 48 inputs agree under the pinned semantics; broader claims need more evidence

items.why: Finite evidence must keep its domain and trusted-base limitations visible.
